summary: Sirach 23 begins as a prayer for protection from inner errors, haughty eyes, evil desire, gluttony, lust, and a shameless mind. It then teaches students to guard their speech, especially oaths, careless use of the divine Name, gross rudeness, and abusive language. The chapter closes with warnings about sexual betrayal, secrecy, public consequences, and the value of fearing and obeying the Lord.
whyItMatters: This chapter gathers several concerns from Sirach’s first major section: teachability, disciplined speech, desire, hidden conduct, and the fear of the Lord. It shows wisdom as formation of both the mouth and the body, not just possession of ideas.

context.author: Yeshua (Jesus) son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; the Greek translation was made later by his unnamed grandson.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jewish readers in Egypt or the wider diaspora.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC, likely around 180–175 BC; the Greek translation followed after the grandson came to Egypt, commonly understood as 132 BC.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with temple worship, scribal learning, Torah, and Greek-speaking Mediterranean culture shaping the world of the book.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction: prayer, direct address to students, maxims, vivid comparisons, and moral warnings.

outline.heading: Prayer for guarded thought and desire
outline.note: The speaker asks the Lord not to abandon him to harmful counsel, multiplied sin, pride, evil desire, gluttony, lust, or a shameless mind.

outline.heading: Discipline of the mouth
outline.note: The teacher calls the children to listen and warns that sinners, insulters, and the arrogant can be trapped by their own lips.

outline.heading: Oaths and the Name
outline.note: The chapter warns against habitual oaths and continual use of the divine Name, linking careless swearing with sin, calamity, and a damaged household.

outline.heading: Rude and abusive speech
outline.note: Another form of speech is described as deadly, gross, and difficult to correct once it becomes a fixed habit.

outline.heading: Passion and secrecy
outline.note: The teacher turns to uncontrolled passion, especially sexual wrongdoing, and confronts the claim that darkness and walls can hide a person from God.

outline.heading: Adultery and lasting consequences
outline.note: A wife who leaves her husband and bears a child by another man is described as violating law, marriage, and family line, with disgrace extending beyond herself.

outline.heading: The final lesson
outline.note: Those left behind are said to learn that nothing is better than fearing the Lord and heeding the Lord’s commandments; verse 28 is blank in the World English Bible.

keyVerses.text: O Lord, Father and Master of my life, don’t abandon me to their counsel. Don’t let me fall because of them.
keyVerses.why: This opening prayer sets the chapter’s posture: the speaker seeks help before addressing speech, desire, and conduct.

keyVerses.text: Listen, my children, to the discipline of the mouth. He who keeps it will not be caught.
keyVerses.why: This verse states the central concern of the middle section: speech needs training because it can trap a person.

keyVerses.text: A man who goes astray from his own marriage bed says in his heart, “Who sees me? Darkness is around me, and the walls hide me. No one sees me. Of whom am I afraid? The Most High will not remember my sins.”
keyVerses.why: This verse voices the self-deception the chapter challenges: the belief that hidden wrongdoing is truly unseen.

keyVerses.text: And those who are left behind will know that there is nothing better than the fear of the Lord, and nothing sweeter than to heed the commandments of the Lord.
keyVerses.why: The closing lesson ties the warnings back to Sirach’s larger wisdom frame: fear of the Lord and obedience are better than secret indulgence.

themes: fear of the Lord and commandments

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin with prayer instead of advice?
questions.answer: The speaker first asks the Lord for help against harmful counsel, errors, pride, desire, gluttony, lust, and a shameless mind. That matters because the chapter treats wise conduct as something requiring discipline and divine help, not only good intentions.

questions.question: Who are “my children”?
questions.answer: The phrase marks the teacher’s audience as learners under instruction. In Sirach, this kind of address fits the book’s setting as wisdom teaching for students being formed in speech, desire, worship, and ordinary life.

questions.question: What does “discipline of the mouth” mean here?
questions.answer: In this chapter it means trained, guarded speech. The verses that follow warn about lips, oaths, naming the Holy One, gross rudeness, and abusive language, so the concern is not silence in general but speech that avoids destructive habits.

questions.question: Is the chapter forbidding every oath?
questions.answer: The wording focuses on becoming accustomed to oaths and continually uttering the Name. Readers differ on how broadly to apply that warning, but within this chapter the emphasis is clearly on habitual, careless, or false swearing that brings sin and calamity.

questions.question: What is “the Name”?
questions.answer: In this chapter, “the Name” refers to the divine Name, connected with “the Holy One” in the previous verse. The warning assumes that speech about God is not casual; repeated misuse of holy language is treated as morally dangerous.

questions.question: Why does Sirach connect rude speech with parents and public company?
questions.answer: Verse 14 pictures a person sitting among great men and becoming a fool through bad habit. Remembering father and mother here seems tied to honor, shame, and the public consequences of speech; the chapter warns that abusive language can become so fixed that it is not corrected.

questions.question: Why does the chapter say darkness and walls do not hide a person?
questions.answer: The adulterer in verse 18 thinks secrecy protects him: no one sees, and the Most High will not remember. The next verses answer that the Lord sees all human ways and secret places, so hiddenness from people is not hiddenness from God.

questions.question: Why are the sexual warnings so severe?
questions.answer: The chapter treats sexual betrayal as more than a private act. It describes damage to marriage, law, children, memory, and public reputation. Some statements reflect an ancient patriarchal household world, so modern readers should notice the power assumptions while still hearing the chapter’s core warning about secrecy, betrayal, and consequences.

questions.question: What does “fear of the Lord” mean at the end?
questions.answer: Here it is paired with heeding the commandments of the Lord. In Sirach’s wider teaching, the phrase points to reverent allegiance shown in conduct, not mere panic. In this chapter, it is presented as the better path after warnings about speech, desire, and hidden wrongdoing.

glossary.def: In this chapter, a harsh image for corrective discipline over thought and for the consequences connected with repeated oaths.
A proud or arrogant outlook; the speaker asks God not to give him this disposition.
A solemn form of speech that calls on a higher authority; this chapter warns against becoming accustomed to it.
A reverent way of referring to God’s name; the chapter warns against continually uttering it in careless speech.
A person characterized here by uncontrolled sexual desire and wrongdoing.
Reverent allegiance to the Lord, shown here by heeding the commandments of the Lord.
